prompt: Which bird will end up at position 3?

solutions.title: Follow each path
solutions.body:
Start at each bird and trace its grey path with your finger all the way down, without jumping to another path at the crossings. The path of the purple bird (B) ends at position 3.

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Work backwards
solutions.body:
Start at position 3 and follow the path **upwards**. It leads to the second bird from the left, the purple one.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: A laser beam reflects in mirrors in the way shown in the small picture. At which letter will this laser beam exit the rectangle?
Rossitza has ten coins in a grid as shown. Which coin does she need to move so that each row and each column has exactly two coins in it?
What is the smallest number of boxes that Bill has to move to be able to open the TRAIN box?

solutions.title: What lies on the TRAIN box?
solutions.body:
The TRAIN box carries two boxes: the stuffed animals box and the bedding box.

- To lift the stuffed animals box, first remove the books box and the music sheets box on top of it.
- The music sheets box also rests on the bedding box. The bedding box also carries the board games box, which must be removed too.

So Bill must move: books, music sheets, board games, stuffed animals and bedding — **5** boxes.

**Answer: (C) 5**

solutions.title: Remove from the top down
solutions.body:
Top layer: books, music sheets, board games (3 boxes) — each of them is on the stuffed animals or the bedding box. Middle layer: stuffed animals and bedding (2 boxes), both lying on the TRAIN box. Total $3 + 2 = 5$. (Cloths, CDs, puzzles and BOOKS don't need to move.)

**Answer: (C) 5**

prompt: Anna makes a jigsaw where any two squares with a common side do not contain the same number. Which piece should she use to complete her jigsaw?
Mario is putting the six puzzle pieces together to make a rectangular picture. Which picture will he get?

solutions.title: Find the all-green piece
solutions.body:
The six pieces make a rectangle of 3 pieces by 2 pieces. One of the pieces is **completely dark green**, and its straight edges show it is a corner piece: so one corner sixth of the picture has no grey at all. In (A) the top-left sixth is all green. In (E) the grey triangle reaches into both top corner pieces, and in (B), (C) and (D) the grey also reaches into every corner part of the picture or the all-grey and half-grey pieces would not fit.

Putting the pieces together — the all-green piece top left, the mostly grey piece at the bottom in the middle, and the pieces with one diagonal edge of grey around them — gives exactly the triangle in (A).

**Answer: (A)**

solutions.title: Follow the grey edges
solutions.body:
On each piece, the border between grey and green is a straight line. When the pieces are put together these lines must continue straight from piece to piece, forming the three sides of the grey triangle. Matching the bumps and holes, the lines form a triangle with its base along the bottom and its top corner to the right of the middle, as in (A).

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: Kengu always makes one large jump followed by two small jumps on the number line, as shown in the picture. Kengu starts at 0 and ends on 11. What is the number of jumps that Kengu makes?

solutions.title: List the landing points
solutions.body:
The large jump is 2 units long and the small jumps are 1 unit. Starting at 0: 2, 3, 4 (3 jumps), 6, 7, 8 (6 jumps), 10, 11 (8 jumps). He reaches 11 after **8** jumps.

**Answer: (C) 8**

solutions.title: Use groups of jumps
solutions.body:
Each group of 3 jumps moves him $2 + 1 + 1 = 4$ units. After 2 groups (6 jumps) he is at 8. Then a large jump to 10 and a small jump to 11: $6 + 2 = 8$ jumps.

**Answer: (C) 8**

prompt: John builds the tower shown. What will he see if he looks at his tower from above?
Mosif wanted the sum of the three numbers in each row and in each column of the grid to be the same. He made one mistake. Which number must he correct?

solutions.title: Add rows and columns
solutions.body:
Rows: $9+1+5 = 15$, $2+7+6 = 15$, $4+8+4 = 16$. Columns: $9+2+4 = 15$, $1+7+8 = 16$, $5+6+4 = 15$. The bottom row and the middle column are too big, and they share the number **8**. Changing 8 into 7 makes all sums 15.

**Answer: (E) 8**

solutions.title: One number, one row, one column
solutions.body:
A single wrong number spoils exactly one row and one column. The wrong row is the bottom one and the wrong column the middle one; the number in both is 8.

**Answer: (E) 8**

prompt: Wanda chose a few of the following shapes and said: "Amongst the shapes I have chosen, there are 3 coloured ones, 2 large ones and 2 round ones." What is the smallest number of shapes that Wanda could have chosen?

solutions.title: Start with the round ones
solutions.body:
There are exactly 2 round shapes (the big white circle and the small red circle), so she took both. That gives 1 large and 1 coloured shape. She needs 1 more large and 2 more coloured shapes, without more circles. The big red square is large and coloured; then she still needs one more coloured shape: the small red triangle. Total: **4** shapes.

**Answer: (C) 4**

solutions.title: Why not 3?
solutions.body:
With 3 shapes, two are the circles, and the third would have to give both one more large **and two** more coloured shapes — impossible with a single shape. So she needs at least 4, and 4 works (two circles, big red square, small red triangle).

**Answer: (C) 4**

prompt: The ages of a family of kangaroos are 2, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 years. The sum of the ages of four of them is 19 years. What are the ages of the other two kangaroos?

solutions.title: Use the total
solutions.body:
All ages together: $2+4+5+6+8+10 = 35$. The other two kangaroos are $35 - 19 = 16$ years together. The pair with sum 16 is 6 and 10.

**Answer: (E) 6 and 10**

solutions.title: Check
solutions.body:
Without 6 and 10: $2 + 4 + 5 + 8 = 19$ ✔.

**Answer: (E) 6 and 10**

prompt: There are five empty cells as shown. You place the five tiles so that the red line forms one continuous line. What tile is in the middle?

solutions.title: Build the line from the half-circle
solutions.body:
Tile (A) has a half-circle that starts and ends on its **left** edge, so it must be the last tile on the right, with two lines coming into it. Only tile (B) sends out two lines on its right side, so (B) is fourth. Its two lines must come from tile (D): the arc of (D) ends at the upper line and its straight line continues to the lower line. So (D) is third, in the middle. Then (C) (one straight line) and (E) (an arc going down) complete the line on the left: E, C, D, B, A.

**Answer: (D)**

solutions.title: Count the line ends
solutions.body:
One continuous line has just two free ends. The tiles have free ends where the red line meets the outer border of the row: the bottom of the arc in (E) and the top of the arc in (D). Arranging E, C, D, B, A connects everything into one line: start at the bottom of E, go right through C and D (straight), through the lower line of B, round the half-circle of A, back along the upper line of B, and up the arc of D. The middle tile is (D).

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Aaron has a square carpet. There are the same number of dots, arranged in two lines, along each side of his carpet. Unfortunately, the carpet has folded. How many dots are there on Aaron's carpet?

Five cars numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 are moving in the direction indicated by the arrow. First, the last car (5) overtakes the two cars ahead of it. Next, the second-last car overtakes the two cars ahead of it. Finally, the middle car overtakes the car ahead of it. In what order are the cars now?

solutions.title: Do the moves one by one
solutions.body:
Start: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (car 1 in front).

1. Car 5 passes 4 and 3: 1, 2, 5, 3, 4.
2. The second-last car is now 3; it passes 5 and 2: 1, 3, 2, 5, 4.
3. The middle car is now 2; it passes only the car ahead of it (3): **1, 2, 3, 5, 4**.

**Answer: (A)**

solutions.title: Use cards
solutions.body:
Lay five numbered cards in a row and move them as described. Be careful: in the last step the middle car passes only **one** car. The cards end up as 1, 2, 3, 5, 4.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: The cube in the picture is built from the three kinds of wooden blocks shown. How many white wooden blocks are used?
In the addition shown, some ink fell on four of the digits so we cannot see them: a three-digit number plus a three-digit number ending in 6 3 gives 572. What is the sum of these four hidden digits?

solutions.title: Column by column
solutions.body:
Ones column: hidden digit $+ 3$ ends in 2, so the hidden digit is 9 (and we carry 1).

Tens column: hidden digit $+ 6 + 1$ ends in 7, so the hidden digit is 0 (no carry).

Hundreds column: the two hidden digits add up to 5.

Sum of the four hidden digits: $9 + 0 + 5 = 14$.

**Answer: (E) 14**

solutions.title: Use the whole numbers
solutions.body:
The bottom number is $\square 63$, i.e. some hundreds plus 63. The top number is $572 - (\text{hundreds} + 63) = 509 - \text{hundreds}$, for example 409 (with 163), 309 (with 263), ... Its tens digit is always 0 and its ones digit 9, and the two hundreds digits add up to 5: total $5 + 0 + 9 = 14$.

**Answer: (E) 14**

prompt: Joanna folds the number square twice as shown. Then she punches a hole through the black spot shown by the arrow. Which numbers does she punch through?

Three football teams participate in a sports tournament. Each team plays the other two teams exactly once. In each game, the winning team gets 3 points and the losing team does not get any points. If the game finishes in a draw, each team gets 1 point. At the end of the tournament, which number of points is it impossible for any team to have?
A pyramid is built from cubes with a side length of 8 cm. An ant climbed up and over the pyramid, as shown by the red line. What is the length of the path walked by the ant?

solutions.title: Up, across, down
solutions.body:
The pyramid has 3 layers, so the ant climbs $3\times 8 = 24$ cm up and $24$ cm down. The view from above shows that all the flat pieces together cross the whole bottom layer, which is 3 cubes wide: $24$ cm. Total $24 + 24 + 24 = 72$ cm.

**Answer: (C) 72 cm**

solutions.title: Count cube edges
solutions.body:
Every piece of the red line is one cube edge long. Going up: 3 edges, across the top steps and the top cube: 3 edges in total (the width of the base), going down: 3 edges. That's 9 edges of 8 cm: $9\times 8 = 72$ cm.

**Answer: (C) 72 cm**

prompt: Alma wants to put one of the pieces 1 to 5 in the middle of the picture so that house A is connected by road to houses B and E, but not to house D. She can rotate the pieces. Which two pieces could she use?

Ahmad and Zhaleh start walking from point A with the same speed, in the directions shown. Ahmad walks around the square-shaped garden. Zhaleh walks around the rectangular-shaped one. What is the smallest number of laps that Zhaleh could do around the rectangular garden to meet Ahmad at point A again?

solutions.title: Lengths of the laps
solutions.body:
Ahmad's lap: $4\times5 = 20$ m. Zhaleh's lap: $10 + 5 + 10 + 5 = 30$ m. They are both at A when each has walked whole laps: Ahmad after 20, 40, **60**, ... m and Zhaleh after 30, **60**, ... m. The first common distance is 60 m, which is **2** laps for Zhaleh.

**Answer: (B) 2**

solutions.title: Check 1 lap
solutions.body:
After 1 lap Zhaleh has walked 30 m, while Ahmad has done $1\tfrac12$ laps — he is on the far side of his garden. After 2 laps (60 m) Ahmad has done exactly 3 laps and is at A too.

**Answer: (B) 2**

prompt: Five children ate some plums. Sophie ate two plums more than Lauren. Betty ate three plums fewer than Sophie. Claire ate one plum more than Betty and three plums fewer than Alice. Which two girls ate the same number of plums?

solutions.title: Compare with Lauren
solutions.body:
- Sophie = Lauren + 2
- Betty = Sophie − 3 = Lauren − 1
- Claire = Betty + 1 = **Lauren**
- Alice = Claire + 3 = Lauren + 3

**Answer: (A) Claire and Lauren**

solutions.title: Try a number
solutions.body:
Say Lauren ate 4 plums: Sophie 6, Betty 3, Claire 4, Alice 7. Claire and Lauren both ate 4.

**Answer: (A) Claire and Lauren**

prompt: A farmer has nine bags of potatoes, as shown. The numbers on the bags show their weights in kilograms. He wants to split them into three groups of three bags each so that each group weighs the same as the others. Which of the following bags will be in the same group as the bag that weighs 6 kilograms?

solutions.title: Find the group weight
solutions.body:
Total: $1+2+3+4+5+6+9+13+17 = 60$ kg, so each group weighs 20 kg.

- The 17 kg bag needs two bags with 3 kg together: 1 and 2. Group: 17, 1, 2.
- The 13 kg bag needs 7 kg more from the remaining 3, 4, 5, 6, 9: only $3 + 4$. Group: 13, 3, 4.
- The rest: 5, 6, 9 = 20 ✔.

The 6 kg bag is with 5 kg and **9 kg**.

**Answer: (D) 9**

solutions.title: Start from the 6
solutions.body:
The 6 kg bag needs 14 kg from two other bags: $5 + 9$ or $1 + 13$. If it took 1 and 13, the 17 would need 3 kg from two bags among 2, 3, 4, 5, 9 — impossible. So it takes 5 and 9 (and then 17+1+2 and 13+3+4 work).

**Answer: (D) 9**

prompt: Which of the following nets could be folded to a cube like this (one face of the cube is made of two triangles)?

solutions.title: Where do the triangles go?
solutions.body:
In each net, the row of four squares wraps around the cube and the square on top becomes the lid. The two triangles must fold under the cube and together cover the bottom face exactly, meeting along a diagonal.

A triangle attached to a side face covers the half of the bottom next to that side, cut by one of the diagonals. The two triangles must be the two different halves of the bottom, cut by the **same** diagonal.

- In (B) the triangles hang below the 1st and 3rd squares (two opposite sides). Both have their right angle on the left, so they are the two halves of the bottom cut by the same diagonal, and fit together.
- In (A), (C), (D) and (E) the two triangles, when folded, overlap or leave a gap (they are cut by different diagonals or cover the same half).

**Answer: (B)**

solutions.title: Make it from paper
solutions.body:
Copy the nets onto paper, cut them out and fold. Only net (B) closes up: its two triangles meet edge to edge on the bottom face and form one square divided by a diagonal, like the cube in the picture.

**Answer: (B)**
